title: The IC Ending
kidRule: When a word with two or more beats ends with the sound 'ik', it is spelled I-C with no K, as in FANTASTIC and TRAFFIC. Save C-K for short words like STICK and KICK!
hint: This longer word ends with the sound 'ik'. Does it need a K at the end?
reminder: A longer word that ends with the sound 'ik' is spelled I-C. No K!

check.question: Why does FANTASTIC end with I-C and not I-C-K?
check.correctAnswer: Because longer words that end with the 'ik' sound are spelled I-C, with no K!
distractors: Because the letter T does not like to be near a K
Because C-K is never used at the end of any word

words.sent: We had a fantastic time at the water park.
words.story: The word comes from the Greek 'phantastikos', about things you can imagine, and it is a cousin of the word 'fantasy'!
words.card: The *fan* blew my hat away, and a *fantastic* seagull brought it back!

words.def: All the cars, trucks, and buses moving along a road.
words.sent: We were late because the traffic was so slow.
words.story: The first electric traffic light was put up in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1914. It had only red and green lights!
words.card: A gi*raff*e stopped the *traffic* by poking its head into a bus!

words.sent: You did a terrific job on your science poster.
words.story: Long ago this word meant 'frightening'. Over time people began to use it for anything big and exciting, and now it means 'great'!
words.card: My sis*ter* baked a *terrific* cake shaped like a turtle!

words.def: Able to pull iron or steel toward it.
words.sent: The magnetic letters stuck to the refrigerator door.
words.story: The Earth acts like one giant magnet, and that is why a compass needle points north!
words.card: My *magnet* is so *magnetic* that it pulled the spoon right out of my soup!

words.def: Strong, fit, and good at sports.
words.sent: The athletic girl ran three laps without stopping.
words.story: The word comes from the Greek 'athlon', which meant a prize. The first athletes were people who competed to win a prize!
words.card: *Let* the *athletic* snail race! He has trained for a whole year!

words.def: Having to do with science, or done in the careful way of science.
words.sent: We did a scientific test to see which paper airplane flew farthest.
words.story: Every kind of living thing has a two-part scientific name. Ours is Homo sapiens, which means 'wise human'!
words.card: The *scient*ist did a *scientific* study to find the yummiest cookie!

words.sent: A majestic eagle soared above the valley.
words.story: The majestic bald eagle is the national bird of the United States, and its wings can stretch about seven feet across!
words.card: The *majestic* lion told a *jest*, and the whole jungle groaned!

words.def: Full of energy and always on the go.
words.sent: The energetic puppy ran around the yard all morning.
words.story: Hummingbirds are so energetic that their wings can beat more than 50 times every second!
words.card: *Get* ready! The *energetic* kangaroo wants to play hopscotch again!

words.def: From a time very long ago, before people wrote things down.
words.sent: We saw the bones of a prehistoric sea creature at the museum.
words.story: Prehistoric artists painted horses, deer, and bulls on the walls of the Lascaux cave in France about 17,000 years ago!
words.card: The *prehistoric* caveman lost *his* sock, so he wore a leaf!

words.def: Very excited and eager about something.
words.sent: The enthusiastic fans cheered for both teams.
words.story: The word 'enthusiasm' comes from Greek. Long ago it described someone so inspired that they seemed to be filled with a special spirit!
words.card: All of *us* were *enthusiastic* about the giant pancake tower!
